title: Lesson 59 - Multi-Agent or Single Agent: Choosing the Architecture and Counting the Cost
description: Given a scenario, determine whether a Multi Agent architecture is appropriate for scalability and control.

questions.question: Sales and support both read the same account records and call the same Flows. The support team asks for its own agent. Following the single-versus-multi-agent decision, what is the better answer?
options: Keep one agent and add a support Subagent with its Actions
Split into two agents and connect them with an orchestrator
Split into two agents and use A2A between them
Move the support team to a different Salesforce org
questions.explanation: When the process shares one data boundary and one domain, the decision framework favours a single agent with a new Subagent and its Actions rather than a new agent and an orchestrator.

questions.question: A team splits a working single agent into an orchestrator and three specialists. Which outcome should they expect?
options: Lower latency because the specialists work in parallel
Lower cost per turn because each agent does less
Higher latency and higher cost per turn because each agent runs its own reasoning loop and orchestration adds a hop
questions.explanation: Each agent runs its own reasoning loop and orchestration adds a hop, so splitting raises latency and the number of model calls behind one user message.

questions.question: Which situation genuinely justifies splitting a single agent into multi-agent orchestration?
options: The requirement spans two business topics
The instruction block is long but still routes correctly
The team wants a tidier architecture diagram
The needed data, workflows, and permissions live in a different Salesforce org
questions.explanation: A data boundary wall, where the needed data and permissions live in a different org or system, is one of the named walls that earns the architectural change, while topic count and tidiness do not.
